Poem of Gilgameš – Old Babylonian Schøyen₂: “Gilgameš Was Lying Down At Rest”

  • API: https://www.ebl.lmu.de/api/texts/L/1/4/chapters/Old%20Babylonian/Sch%C3%B8yen%E2%82%82/display

1a

  • N: gilgāmeš | sakip | nīl
  • T: Gilgameš was lying down at rest;
  • L: gilgāmeš ← Gilgameš I; sakip ← sakāpu II “to rest, lie down Bab.”; nīl ← nâlu I “to lie down (to sleep)”

6

  • N: šadûm | iqūpam-ma | iseʾʾân[ni]
  • T: the mountain collapsed on me, pressing me down.
  • L: šadûm ← šadû I “st. constr. šad(i)”; iqūpam-ma ← qâpu I “to fall down, collapse Bab., NA”; iseʾʾân[ni] ← se'û I “~ to press down M/jB part of liver, of body”
  • Note: See [RN127: 34a]: “The second verb was formerly understood as īsiḫanni from esēḫum “to gird”. The parsing from seʾû “to push down”, a verb not previously encountered in Old Babylonian, is the suggestion of [khait2006observations: 530], who understood it as perfect. I take it as present, iseʾʾânni, describing the result of the mountain’s collapse.”

8

  • N: ahīya | šalummatum | uddannin
  • T: a radiant brightness overpowered my arms.
  • L: ahīya ← ahu II “arm, side (st. constr. ah(i))”; šalummatum ← šalummatu I “~ radiance Bab., Bogh., Ug. of deities, king, temple, cult…”; uddannin ← danānu I “power, strength O/jB, M/NA of god, king, enemy”
  • Note: See [RN127: 34a]: “For dunnunum in the sense “to overpower” rather than “to strengthen”, see another dream account, SB Gilgameš VII 171: iṣbat qimmātīya udanninanni yâši “he took hold of my hair, he was too strong for me” (Khait and Nurullin, private communication).”

BabaOB1 o 8. a-hi-ia ša-lum-ma-tum# ud-da-an-ni-in

9

  • N: ištēn | eṭlum || lābiš | [iṭh]eam
  • T: There was a man, like a lion [he drew] near me,
  • L: ištēn ← ištēn I “f. išteat, ištiat, iš/ltē/īt(um), iš/ltât, NA issēt”; eṭlum ← eṭlu I “manly”; lābiš ← lābu I “lion”; [iṭh]eam ← ṭehû I “to be(come) near to, approach”
  • Note: See [RN127: 34]: “Previously I read labiš [pal]âm “clad in a royal mantle”. This can still be defended but there are other possibilities. Khait and Nurullin suggest la-bi-i[š it-b]é-a-am and translate “arose (to me) like a lion” ([khait2006observations: 531]). In the context of wild animals tebûm is a verb of aggression, meaning “to rear up, attack”. The figure in the dream comes to Gilgameš’s aid, however, and lābiš tebûm is not in keeping. Khait and Nurullin’s parsing of lābiš as a modal adverb is a good one, however, adding a further example of such a formation in Old Babylonian to those identified by W. G. Lambert and collected by [RN2175: 171 fn. 28]. If it is the correct parsing the last word of the line is to be reconstructed as a verb, as they saw, but as [iṭ-ḫ]e-a-am rather than [it-b]é-a-am. The broken sign is a better ḫe than bé, and the verb ṭeḫûm is less aggressive than tebûm.”
  • Parallels: cf. L I.4 MB "Boğ₂" 15'b
BabaOB1 o 9. iš-te-en eṭ-lum la-bi-iš# [iṭ-h]e-a-am

18

  • N: parṣam | ša mutim || šipirti (|) zikari
  • T: the rite of a warrior, the task of a man.
  • L: parṣam ← parṣu I “office”; ša ← ša I “who(m), which”; mutim ← mutu I “m.”; šipirti ← šipirtu I “pl. šip(i)rātu(m), šip(i)rētu message, letter, instruction Bab.,…”; zikari ← zikaru I “male, virile stat. is manly”
  • Note: See [RN127: 34–35]: “My former decipherment of the first sign overlooked the fact that the sign BAR was already used with the value pár (very rarely) in the Old Babylonian period. The revised reading and the recovery of the whole line are owed to the brilliance of Khait and Nurullin, who caught the sense of the line and made me revisit it. They read the line as parṣam ša mutim piširti ikkari and translated “a ritual of a man, an exorcism of a ploughman”, noted a parallelism between parṣum and pišertum, mutum and ikkarum and commented that the line offered “an explanation of ištiāt ‘something unique’ that Gilgamesh was supposed to make when he would meet Ḫuwawa, but we can say nothing about its exact meaning” ([khait2006observations: 532]). What happens when Gilgameš met Ḫuwawa was a titanic struggle so violent that the very mountain split asunder, and the logical conclusion is that the enigmatic parṣam ša mutim and the phrase that follows it allude this extraordinary act of single combat. The former phrase is easier to explain. It evokes the noble sentiment that warfare is a socio-religious duty or rite (parṣum) for able-bodied young men (mutum). This sentiment permeates ancient Mesopotamian literature: in an Old Babylonian poem about Sargon the prospect of battle is articulated by the line [i]-si-nu-um ša mu-ti in-né-pu-uš “the festival of warriors will take place” (ed. [RN262: 62 l. 19]); in Lugale 136 battle is ezen nam.guruš.a // i-sin-ni eṭ-lu-ti “the festival of young men”; in Erra I 51 it is said that a-lak ṣēri(edin) ša eṭ-lu-ti ki-i šá i-sin-nu-um-ma “the young men’s departure for the battlefield is like a time of festival”. Warfare is also described as isinnum “a festival” in the Agušaya poem ([RN1217: 76 iii 7 // 11]) and the Tukultī-Ninurta epic ([RN19: 99 iiia 20, 106 v 11]). While the second of the two phrases is so damaged that the reading pišerti ikkari cannot be excluded on orthographic grounds, it seemed to me on collation that a better semantic parallel with parṣam ša mutim can be obtained by reading instead šipirti zikari. In this phrase šipirtum is a synonym of šiprum “task, duty”, and thus restates parṣum but in a more mundane and less idealized way; zikarum is likewise a synonym of mutum, but less literary. In this way the line juxtaposes two phrases that display Babylonian idealism and practice respectively.”

38

  • N: ana rigim (|) adad | ennešu | anāku
  • T: At the sound of Adad I grew bewildered,
  • L: ana ← ana I “(aš-š... etc.) to, for (freq. abbr. an, with assimilation of n…”; rigim ← rigmu I “pl. f. voice, cry, noise voice of deity, human”; adad ← Adad I; ennešu ← enēšu I “to be(come) weak”; anāku ← anāku I “I”
  • Note: See [RN127: 35–36]: “The sign before anāku was revealed after cleaning to comprise only three wedges, discounting both my former decipherment en-ni-iš and Khait and Nurullin’s en-né-ṭù ([khait2006observations: 532–3]). I now parse the word in question from ešûm. This verb is conventionally booked as i/i class, so that the IV/1 preterite 1.sg. is expected to be enneši, as indeed it is in the Old Babylonian Narām-Sîn legend iii 8: a-na-ku es-⸢se-hi⸣ en-né-ši “I grew confused and bewildered” (ed. Westenholz 1997: 272). The late version of this text has instead forms with final /u/: in l. 88 the indicative es-se-hu en-né-šú and in l. 154 the negative imperative la te-(es5)-se-eh-hu la te-en-neš-šú “be not confused, be not bewildered” (ed. Gurney 1955, cf. Westenholz 1997: 318, 326 l. 156). The sources of the late version are tablets from Sultantepe, where an unexpected quality of final vowel would usually be shrugged off, and from Nineveh, where wrong stem vowels in final position are rare but not unknown (e.g. [RN117: 441 sub t]). However, the spelling te-es₅*-se-eh-hu* in l. 154 (MS C, Nineveh) retains in IŠ = es₅ a peculiarly Old Babylonian value, so that perhaps the spellings are there faithful to a second-millennium forerunner. Given the present attestation, on an Old Babylonian tablet, of ennešu instead of enneši, it looks as if there was indeed a time when ešûm was sometimes conjugated as a verb of the u/u class. Another case of a verb exhibiting both /u/ and /i/ in final position occurs in the next line.”

  • Note: On ēmi for ēma, see [RN117: 240]. See also [RN127: 36a]: “The decipherment i-⸢ṭù⸣-ma u₄*-mu* and its translation as “the day went dark” presume OB eṭûm exhibits a vowel class III-u; the phrase should be compared with i-DI u₄-mu in three first-millennium copies of Ludlul II 119, understood as īṭi ūmu by Landsberger and others: see especially Cooper 1975. Unless the phrase in the present line is plural, i.e. īṭûma ūmū (which seems improbable), this rare verb evidently exhibits both /u/ and /i/ in final position. It might thus be added to those that switched vowel classes over time (cf. GAG §87bd), but this cannot be confirmed without further attestations.” See also [NABU2004-49].

  • N: adī-ma | kīam-ma | šuppūtum | ibteli | išātum
  • T: At long last(?) the fire that flared so high died down,
  • L: adī-ma ← adi I “until, as far as”; kīam-ma ← kīam I “so, thus”; šuppūtum ← šapû II “to be dense”; ibteli ← belû II “to be extinguished, come to an end O/jB, NA”; išātum ← išātu I “f.”
  • Note: See [RN117: 240]: “The first half of the line is the counterpart of the later version’s [idʾ]imma, which suggests that adīma kīʾamma at some point in the tradition ceased to be understood. Literally it means ‘as far as so’. Shorn of enclitics the phrase appears several times elsewhere: BIN 4 228, 9: a-di ki-a-am wa#-aš₂#-ba#-a#-ku, TCL XX 117, 15: a-di ki-a-am a-we-lum₂ ha-am-da-tim iš-pu-ra-kum (both OA letters), VAS XVI 131,6 (ed. AbB VI 131): a-di ki-a-am be₂-re-e a-na mi-ni ta-al-li-ik (OB letter). In the Old Assyrian letters the expression adi kīʾam means ‘for that reason’ or similar, in the Babylonian example perhaps ‘for so many’ (I am grateful to K. R. Veenhof for his thoughts on these passages, communicated privately). Neither rendering fits the present instance and I have translated ad hoc. The adjective written šu-up-pu-tum, replaced by nebūtu in the late text, can be derived from the II/1 stem of šapû A, ‘to flare up’, or IIl/1 stem of nabû C, ‘to shine brightly’; either way it is an elative. I have opted for the former parsing, in view of nablū išpû in I. 37. For nouns that occur separated from their adjectives and for the reversal of the conventional order, noun + adjective, see Ch. 9, the section on Some features of language and style.”
  • Parallels: cf. L I.4 SB "IV" 105
